https://www.politico.eu/article/who-ware.text: A World Health Organization (WHO) warehouse storing emergency health supplies in Ukraine has been destroyed, as Kyiv and Moscow exchanged fresh missile strikes overnight, causing several deaths and leaving tens of people injured. Russia launched a “massive” strike on Odesa overnight, according to Ukrainian emergency services, with at least eight people injured. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an X post on Sunday that the “brutal strike” on the city targeted energy infrastructure as well as residential buildings and the port. A separate Russian strike on the Saltivka district of Kharkiv killed two people and injured at least 21 more, according to the head of the region’s state administration. Ukraine’s emergency services said firefighters rescued seven people from the upper floors of a high-rise building. Advertisement Advertisement Another overnight strike on the Zhytomyr region injured three people, Ukrainian emergency services said. Meanwhile, five people died in a Ukrainian overnight drone attack on the Russian city of Belgorod, the regional crisis centre said on Sunday. Acting governor Alexander Shuvayev said earlier on Sunday that three people were killed and 25 others injured in the “massive terrorist drone attack” by Kyiv. The death toll later rose to five. Zelenskyy condemned what he described as “ballistic terror” attacks on Odesa, Kharkiv, Pavlohrad, and other regions. “Every such attack on human life serves as a constant reminder – we need more pressure, more sanctions against Russia, and more air defense for Ukraine,” he said. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director-general of the World Health Organization, said on Sunday that a WHO warehouse in Dnipro in Ukraine was destroyed by a strike on Friday. The warehouse held humanitarian supplies for frontline health facilities. No casualties were reported, as a WHO staff member and drivers managed to evacuate 130 of approximately 300 pallets and left the area before the attack. “I cannot say loudly enough: attacks on health care MUST STOP. Otherwise, people are deprived of lifesaving healthcare,” Tedros said. Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: Sarah Young/Reuters View image in fullscreen BAE Systems unveils its unmanned fighter aircraft Brontanax in July. BAE voluntarily disclosed all but one of the alleged violations by its US arm. Photograph: Sarah Young/Reuters BAE Systems BAE Systems to pay $36m penalty after 104 violations of US arms export rules State department says it has reached administrative settlement with company’s US arm to resolve breaches Graeme Wearden Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.35 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK defence company BAE Systems is to pay a $36m (£26.7m) civil penalty after breaching US arms exports regulations more than 100 times. The US Department of State announced on Thursday that it had reached an administrative settlement with the US arm of BAE to resolve 104 violations of the Arms Export Control Act and the International Traffic in Arms Regulations. The breaches included the unauthorised exports of technical data to multiple countries, including China, and violations of directorate of defense trade controls authorisations involving various countries. BAE voluntarily disclosed all but one of the alleged violations, which helped it avoid a higher penalty. It also persuaded the state department to suspend half of the penalty, on the condition that the $18m was used to strengthen BAE’s compliance programme. BAE Systems said it remained committed to ensuring full compliance with all applicable export control laws, and had “thoroughly cooperated” with the state department’s review. “We have been working diligently to implement improvements to our BAE Systems Inc compliance programme over the last several years, and we will continue to do so. We take seriously our responsibility to protect critical information and support all our customers’ security,” the company added. The state department said the settlement highlighted “the importance of exporting defence articles pursuant only to appropriate authorisation from the department”. BAE was accused of sending technical data related to printed wiring boards for use in global positioning system (GPS) to a manufacturer in China in December 2023. According to the state department, the company “recognised its supply chain team did not fully understand the export control and compliance regulations” and that its secure file transfer networks did not highlight export control warnings before the data was sent. The company also sent data related to printed wiring boards for use with military GPS to Canada in September 2021, after a licence agreement had expired, and the technical specification of an “explosive mixture” to the UK. In another breach, technical data related to a US navy guided-missile destroyer were sent to Germany. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion A BAE subcontractor also “furnished defence services without authorisation” on more than 17 separate occasions in Italy and France, and also in Indonesia, according to the state department. The company also accidentally exported without authorization a control system for a military gas-turbine engine to Switzerland. https://www.politico.eu/article/national.text: DUBLIN — The leaders of the three nationalist parties that want to break up the United Kingdom have signed a joint agreement to coordinate their rebel ambitions. Monday’s signing ceremony by the Scottish National Party , Ireland’s Sinn Féin and Wales’ Plaid Cymru creates a fresh headache for U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham — who’s already on the constitutional defensive after the weekend’s surprise intervention by Donald Trump . The nationalist leaders gathering in the Welsh capital, Cardiff — Wales First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth, Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill and Scotland First Minister John Sweeney — offered only a subdued, indirect welcome for Trump’s out-of-the-blue declaration that a united Ireland was “inevitable.” That lack of praise for Trump reflected their shared opposition to his wider policy agenda. Advertisement Advertisement But all three agreed that Trump’s sentiments reinforced their own sense that the time was right for independence referendums in Scotland and Ireland, and a push for greater devolution of powers from Westminster to the Welsh Assembly. “Each of our nations has the right to determine its own future, through democratic means and in accordance with the wishes of its people,” the three parties said in a joint statement . They met in Cardiff to acknowledge the fact that all three devolved administrations in the U.K. are now led by nationalists for the first time following May’s electoral trouncing by Plaid Cymru of Burnham’s Labour, long the party of government in Wales. Sweeney, Scotland’s leader since 2024, is seeking a second independence referendum following the failed 2014 vote . Burnham, who holds the levers on permitting such a ballot, has ruled it out . “I think he [Burnham] will be the last prime minister of the United Kingdom, because the people of Scotland, if given the choice of independence in a referendum, will take that choice,” Sweeney said, citing recent polling trends. Advertisement Advertisement Sinn Féin — which contests elections in both parts of Ireland — has spent nearly three decades appealing for the British government to permit a border poll in Northern Ireland. Sinn Féin wants the north, a part of the U.K., to merge with the Republic of Ireland, which won independence from Britain more than a century ago. Reflecting the party’s more complicated all-Ireland structure, Sinn Féin came to Cardiff represented both by O’Neill, who leads the cross-community government in Northern Ireland, and by party chief Mary Lou McDonald, a Dubliner who leads the opposition in Ireland’s parliament. McDonald — who has boycotted traditional St. Patrick’s Day events at the White House since Trump’s 2024 re-election — billed the president’s pro-unity comment as part of an age-old American sympathy for the Irish, one of the country’s biggest ethnic identities. “It’s surprising that there is surprise that a New Yorker, that an American president, would say that they see the logic, the good sense of unity … the inevitability, as he sees it,” McDonald told reporters. Ireland’s leader, Taoiseach Micheál Martin of the center-ground Fianna Fáil party, didn’t comment on Trump’s intervention as they spent much of the weekend together — but broke his silence Monday to warn that simple-minded calls for unity did more harm than good. Martin avoided mentioning Trump explicitly on that point, instead billing it as a problem for his opponents, Sinn Féin, which spent decades supporting Irish Republican Army violence in Northern Ireland. The main faction, the Provisional IRA, killed nearly 1,800 people from 1970 to 1997, when the outlawed group ceased fire. “I believe in Irish unity, but I want an Irish unity that works. That takes hard work. I’m not into simplistic rhetoric,” Martin told RTÉ radio in Dublin. “I’m not into timelines. I’m not into saying we’ll do it all next week and it’ll be simple. And some of the rhetoric I’m listening to, even Sinn Féin at times, harkening back to the 1970s — I worry about that.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.dailystar.co.uk/news/latest-.text: Four people accused of murdering a baby girl found dead wrapped in a towel and a bag are due to appear before Crown Court for the first time on Thursday. The newborn, named only as Baby S, suffered 33 wounds from 15 seperate stabbings. She was tragically found dead in an outhouse in the Wincobank area of Sheffield on Sunday (August 30). Andrea Skopova, 20, Peter Horvath Jnr, 19, Peter Horvath Snr, 38, and Nina Horvathova, 37, appeared before Sheffield Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday morning charged with the murder of Baby S. They were remanded in custody and will appear at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday. Horvath Jnr, Horvath Snr and Horvathova, all of Holywell Heights, and Skopova, of Robey Street, Grimesthorpe, Sheffield, are also charged with causing or allowing the death of a child, and perverting the course of justice by cleaning the scene of the alleged crime. All the defendants are Slovakian nationals, the court heard. The four adults stood in court wearing identical grey t-shirts and flanked by four security guards. A 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named, appeared at the court later, in a separate hearing, is charged with the same perverting the course of justice offence. The girl sobbed in the dock as representations were made about whether she should be released on bail. District Judge Tim Spruce decided she should be remanded in youth custody until Thursday, when she will appear at crown court with the other defendants. Prosecutor Luke Hopkinson said the baby had suffered 33 wounds from 15 “separate stabbings”. Two women, aged 26 and 37, who were arrested on suspicion of murder remain on bail.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) take part in a protest demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter-roll irregularities. Photograph: Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) take part in a protest demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter-roll irregularities. Photograph: Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty Images This Is India World news Shock, anger and a crackdown: why a contentious electoral revision has sparked outrage Marches in Delhi against changes to voting registration led to dragnets, internet blackouts – and questions about India’s electoral independence. Plus, the cinematographer capturing the beauty of the mundane Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Niha Masih Tue 13 Oct 2026 02.30 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 04.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google M onths of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital. Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown , transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet : 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest. The founders of the Cockroach party were removed from an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were also swept up in the detentions . A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police, his shirt torn in the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations. “I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav, who was also detained , said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence. The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramatic images of police personnel detaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide. The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad accusing the opposition of weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing. While suppression of protests is not new , what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir have been far more severe, particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after the revocation of Article 370 . View image in fullscreen An activist tries to stop a police bus carrying detained protesters during a demo seeking the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner. Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/Reuters The ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process. The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after an Indian Express investigation reported that the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in a Kafkaesque limbo . Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed to benefit the ruling regime . Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as a duty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run. Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissioners legal immunity for actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges. As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.” On Monday, the Keralam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.” What else we’re reading about View image in fullscreen South African jurist and former UN human rights chief Navanethem ‘Navi’ Pillay has won the 2026 Nobel peace prize. Photograph: Daniel Karmann/DPA/AP Human rights | South African jurist and former international criminal court judge, Navi Pillay , who is of Indian Tamil heritage, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a first-person account published in 2023 , she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land. Technology | The United States has suspended labour-certification processing for several major technology companies, including top Indian IT firms , as part of a crackdown on what it alleges is a misuse of its flagship green card program, fraud and the displacement of American workers. The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week. Climate | Citing a significant rainfall deficit linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon, the Maharashtra government last week announced water cuts of at least 10% across urban areas starting 16 October. The state government had previously declared drought conditions in 74% of the sub-districts. Guest shelf A recommendation from someone with great taste skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is India Niha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern India after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen The Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. Photograph: Mayank Austen Soofi With Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned to Mayank Austen Soofi , who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.” Count it A number worth knowing View image in fullscreen Koushila Markam holds a photo of her daughter, Bamita Markam, who died from measles during an outbreak in Balaghat. Photograph: BBC News 32 At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June, the Indian Express reported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain. Vibe check View image in fullscreen A quiet moment between Arbab Kamal Khan’s parents, whose everyday intimacy features in his photographs. For Mumbai-based cinematographer, Arbab Kamal Khan , the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance. “When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.” For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – their feet across each other besides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or his dad resting under his wife’s dupatta as she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence. Beállítom „Tegnapi találkozónkon a főpolgármester a kerületi pénzek további elvonásának tervét ismertette. Ezen az úton nem tudjuk követni, mert ez Budapest romlásának az útja” – írja közös, kedden kiadott nyilatkozatában nyolc budapesti polgármester. A nyilatkozatot Baranyi Krisztina ferencvárosi, Pikó András józsefvárosi és Soproni Tamás terézvárosi polgármester is aláírta, akik már korábban is nyilvánosan kikeltek Karácsony ellen. Leginkább azért, mert Karácsony Gergely a hátuk mögött kötött alkut a kormánnyal, amelynek része, hogy a jövőben központosítanák a budapesti parkolást , a főváros szedné ebből a bevételeket, hogy útfelújításokat tudjon csinálni. A polgármesterek a keddi nyilatkozatban arról írtak, Karácsony „ellehetetleníti a kerületekben élő fővárosiak esélyét arra, hogy az utcáik és tereik tisztábbak és biztonságosabbak legyenek, hogy az óvodák és idősotthonok, a kerületi rendelők és a családsegítők legalább az eddig megszokott színvonalon működjenek”. Szerintük túl nagy árat fizet a főpolgármester azért, hogy „előkészítetlenül improvizált, átgondolatlan ötletek miatt felforgassuk a város életét”. A nyilatkozat szerint Budapest csak akkor tud fejlődni, ha „a fővárosi és a kerületi önkormányzatok együtt, egymással szolidáris közösségben dolgoznak”. „A 2019 óta alapvetően jól kooperáló közösség a főpolgármester és a kormány között kötött paktum miatt megbomlott.” A közleményt Baranyi Krisztina (IX. kerület), László Imre (XI. kerület), Niedermüller Péter (VII. kerület), Pikó András (VIII. kerület), Rózsa András (XIV. kerület), Soproni Tamás (VI. kerület) Szaniszló Sándor (XVIII. kerület) és Tóth József (XIII. kerület) polgármester írták alá. https://telex.hu/sport/2026/11/08/szobos.text: Szoboszlai Dominik nincs százszázalékos állapotban, ezért nem játszotta végig a vasárnapi meccset a Crystal Palace ellen Londonban – mondta a Liverpool FC vezetőedzője, Andoni Iraola az MTI szerint. „A legutolsó dolog, amire most szükségünk van, hogy elveszítsünk játékosokat a válogatott szünetben” – fogalmazott Szoboszlaival kapcsolatban. Iraola azt mondta, az előző szünetben három nagyon fontos futballistája tért vissza sérülten. „Most imádkozom, hogy ne így legyen. Szoboszlai térde nincs százszázalékos állapotban, ezért óvatosnak kell lennie. Tudom, hogy ő mindent megtesz annak érdekében, hogy menjen, mert szeret a válogatottban futballozni, de meg kell vizsgálni őt az orvosoknak”. A vezetőedző azt mondta, jobban örülne, ha ezúttal nem szerepelne a válogatottban, de hozzátette, természetesen megértőnek kell lennie, ráadásul tanítványa is szeretne menni. A Liverpool 3-1-re győzött a londoni csapat ellen a brit fővárosban, Kerkez Milos végigjátszotta a mérkőzést, Szoboszlait pedig a 69. percben cserélték le.
